title: Le Horla
author: Guy de Maupassant
blurb: A man's diary by the Seine. His water jug is empty every morning, though he hasn't touched it. Someone else lives in his room.

p: 8 May. What a wonderful day! I spent the whole morning lying on the grass, in front of my house, under the huge plane tree that shades all of it.
I love this region, and I love living here, because it is here that I have my roots, those deep, delicate roots that bind a man to the land where his ancestors were born and died.
My house stands on the bank of the Seine, near Rouen. From my garden, I watch the boats go by.
At around eleven o'clock, a long convoy of ships passed in front of my gate.
Behind them came a superb Brazilian three-master, all white, wonderfully clean and gleaming.
I saluted it, I don't know why; it was such a pleasure to see that ship.
12 May. I've had a slight fever for a few days; I feel unwell, or rather, I feel sad.
Where do they come from, these mysterious influences that turn our happiness into discouragement, and our confidence into anguish?
It's as if the air, the invisible air, were full of forces we don't know, and whose presence we have to endure.
We see so few things! Our eyes cannot make out the very small, nor the very large, nor the very near, nor the very far.
16 May. I really am ill! I have a constant fever, or rather a feverish nervousness, that makes my soul suffer as much as my body.
I constantly have the terrible feeling of a danger threatening me, of a misfortune about to happen.
18 May. I've just been to see my doctor, because I couldn't sleep any more.
He found my pulse fast, but no worrying symptom. I must take showers and potassium bromide.
25 May. No change! My condition really is strange.
Every evening, as night approaches, an incomprehensible unease takes hold of me, as if the night were hiding a terrible threat for me.
I lock my door, I look under my bed, I listen... I listen... for what?
I sleep a little, then I feel, in my sleep, that someone is coming near me, looking at me, touching me, climbing onto my bed, kneeling on my chest and taking my neck in his hands to strangle me.
I want to scream, I can't; I want to move, I can't.
At last I wake up, covered in sweat. I light a candle. I'm alone.
2 June. My condition has got worse again. What on earth is wrong with me?
Yesterday, I went for a walk in the forest of Roumare.
Suddenly, I had the feeling that someone was walking behind me, very close, close enough to touch me.
I spun round, and when I stopped, I no longer knew which way I had come.
3 June. I spent a horrible night. I'm going to go away for a few weeks. A little trip will no doubt set me right.
2 July. I'm home. I'm cured. I had a delightful trip. I visited Mont-Saint-Michel, which I had never seen.
An old monk who was showing me round the abbey told me the legends of the region: voices heard at night on the beach, creatures nobody has ever seen.
'Do you believe in these things?' I asked him.
He answered: 'Do we see a hundred-thousandth part of what exists?
Look at the wind, which is the greatest force in nature. It knocks men down, destroys houses, uproots trees.
Have you ever seen it? And yet it exists.'
I fell silent before this simple reasoning. This man was a wise man, or perhaps a madman.
5 July. Have I lost my mind? What happened last night is so strange that my head swims when I think about it.
As I now do every evening, I had locked my door.
Then, being thirsty, I had drunk half a glass of water, and I had noticed that my jug was full up to the stopper.
I went to bed, and I had my nightmare again. I woke up, terrified, and wanted a drink.
I picked up the jug: it was empty! It was completely empty!
Someone had drunk that water. But who? Me? Surely me? It could only have been me. So I was a sleepwalker...
6 July. I'm going mad. My whole jug was drunk again last night; or rather, I drank it!
But is it me? Is it me? Who could it be? Who? Oh God! Who will save me?
10 July. I've just carried out some astonishing experiments.
Before going to bed, I put wine, milk, water, bread and strawberries on my table.
In the morning, all the water and a little of the milk had been drunk. Nobody had touched the wine, the bread or the strawberries.
The next day, I wrapped the bottles in white cloths, and I rubbed my lips, my beard and my hands with pencil lead.
When I woke up, the cloths were still perfectly white: I hadn't touched them. Yet the water and the milk had been drunk.
So it wasn't me. Someone else was living in my room. Someone I couldn't see.
12 July. Paris. So I had lost my head these last few days!
Twenty-four hours in Paris were enough to give me back my calm. The streets full of people, the cafés, the theatres: all that chases ghosts away.
14 July. Republic Day. I strolled through the streets. The fireworks and the flags amused me like a child.
16 July. Yesterday I saw things that troubled me greatly.
I was dining at my cousin's, Madame Sablé. Among the guests was Doctor Parent, who is very interested in hypnotism.
To show us his power, he put my cousin to sleep in a few minutes, simply by looking into her eyes.
Then he said to her: 'Tomorrow morning at eight o'clock, you will go and see your cousin, and you will ask him for five thousand francs for your husband.'
I went back to my hotel laughing at this charade.
The next morning, at eight o'clock, there was a knock at my door. It was my cousin, very pale, her eyes lowered.
'My dear cousin,' she said to me, 'I have a big favour to ask you. My husband needs five thousand francs, right away.'
I knew that her husband was rich. I looked at her: she wasn't lying; she really believed what she was saying.
Doctor Parent woke her up in the afternoon, and she remembered nothing. She didn't even understand what I was talking about.
I went home convinced that a will from outside can enter us and govern us.
6 August. This time, I'm not mad. I saw... I saw... I saw!
I was walking at two o'clock, in broad sunlight, in my garden, among the rose bushes.
I stopped to look at a magnificent red rose.
Then I saw, I saw distinctly, right next to me, the stem of that rose bend, as if an invisible hand had twisted it, then break, as if that hand had picked it!
Then the flower rose, as if an arm were carrying it towards a mouth, and it stayed hanging in the clear air, all alone, motionless, a terrifying red spot three steps from my eyes.
Beside myself, I threw myself at it to grab it! I found nothing: it had disappeared.
But the broken stem was there, on the rose bush. I hadn't dreamt it.
I am certain now that there exists near me an invisible being, who feeds on milk and water, who can touch things, pick them up and move them.
He lives under my roof. He watches me. He dominates me.
12 August. For the last few days, I've had no will of my own. Someone possesses it and governs it in my place.
I want to leave, to escape, and I can't. I want to go out; I can't.
He doesn't want me to; and I stay, sitting in my armchair, distraught, trembling.
I would only like to stand up, to prove to myself that I'm still my own master. I can't!
16 August. Today I managed to escape for two hours, like a prisoner who by chance finds the door of his prison open.
I suddenly felt that I was free and that he was far away. I ordered my coachman to take me to Rouen, at a gallop.
At the library, I asked for an old book about invisible beings and the spirits that live in the air.
Then, when I wanted to tell the coachman 'To the station!', I shouted, in a voice so loud that the passers-by turned round: 'Home!'
He had found me, and he had taken me back.
17 August. Last night, I saw him. I had read until one in the morning, then I had fallen asleep in my armchair, with the window open.
When I woke up, I saw on my table an open book whose pages were turning by themselves, as if someone sitting in my armchair were reading.
In one leap I threw myself at him, but the armchair fell over, and the window slammed shut, as if a burglar, caught by surprise, had fled.
So he had been afraid, afraid of me, he had!
19 August. I know... I know... I know everything! I've just read this in the Revue du Monde scientifique:
'Some rather curious news reaches us from São Paulo, in Brazil. An epidemic of madness is raging in the region.
The inhabitants claim that they are being pursued by invisible beings, who drink their water and their milk during the night, and who dominate their will.'
Ah! I remember! I remember the beautiful Brazilian three-master that passed under my windows on 8 May!
I had found it so pretty, so white, so cheerful! The Being was on board, coming from over there, where its race was born.
And it saw me! It saw my white house too; and it jumped from the ship onto the bank.

Its name is... it seems to me that it is shouting its name to me, and I can't hear it... Yes... it's shouting it... I'm listening... the... Horla... I heard... the Horla... it's him... the Horla... he has come!
In the evening, I pretended to write, to deceive him. I knew he was there, prowling around me.
In front of me was my big mirrored wardrobe, in which I looked at myself every day to dress.
Suddenly, I stood up and turned round, so fast that I nearly fell.
Well?... It was as bright as day, and I didn't see myself in my mirror!
It was empty, clear, deep, full of light! My reflection wasn't in it... and there I was, right in front of it!
Then I began to make myself out in a mist, at the back of the mirror, as if through a layer of water.
He was there, between the mirror and me. His invisible body had hidden my reflection.
I had seen him! The terror of it has stayed with me, and it still makes me shiver.
10 September. Rouen, Hôtel Continental. It's done... it's done... but is he dead?
I had had iron shutters and an iron door fitted in my room, as if I were afraid of burglars.
Last night, I felt him in my room. I acted as if nothing were wrong, then, all of a sudden, I went out, double-locked the door, and put the key in my pocket.
He was shut in! Then I set fire to the house.
I hid at the bottom of the garden, and I waited.
The flames rose, red and yellow, up to the black sky.
And suddenly, I heard a horrible scream, a woman's scream, coming from the second floor.
My servants! I had forgotten them! I saw their terrified faces at the windows, and their arms waving...
The people of the village came running, but it was too late. The house was nothing but an immense blaze.
But him, him, the Horla? Was he dead?
If his body is made of light and air, perhaps fire can do nothing against him.
We die, we do, because our bodies are fragile. But perhaps he will only die when the world ends.
No... no... without a doubt, without a doubt... he isn't dead...
Then... then... I am going to have to kill myself!...

a-t-elle: she has (a-t-elle dit / demandé = she said / asked)
air: look, air (avoir l'air = to look, seem)
apercevoir: to make out, to perceive (s'apercevoir = to see oneself)
arriver: to manage (y arriver = to manage it)
au: to the, at the, in the
bond: leap, bound (d'un bond = in one leap)
changent: change, turn (changer … en = to turn … into)
chasse: hunting (aller à la chasse = to go hunting)
cher: dearly (coûter cher = to cost a lot)
chez: at the home of (chez eux = at their place)
comme: like, as; how (comme c'est… ! = how … it is!)
connaissais: knew (que je ne connaissais pas = that I'd never seen)
cou: neck (sauter au cou de = to throw your arms round)
couché: gone to bed (je me suis couché)
croyez-vous: do you believe (croire à = to believe in)
côté: side, way (de quel côté = which way)
deviens: am becoming (je deviens fou = I'm going mad)
dire: to say (il faut dire = it must be said)
est-il: is he (est-il mort ? = is he dead?)
fais: am having (je la fais réparer = I'm having it repaired)
faisait: was (weather: il faisait froid = it was cold)
falloir: to be necessary (il va falloir que = I'm going to have to)
fois: time (cette fois = this time; sept cents fois = 700 times)
fond: back, bottom (au fond de = at the bottom of)
frappé: knocked (on a frappé = there was a knock)
jeté: threw (je me suis jeté sur = I threw myself at)
lit: bed (aller au lit = to go to bed)
maison: home, house (à la maison = at home)
maître: master (maître de moi = my own master)
millième: thousandth (la cent millième partie = a hundred-thousandth)
mont-saint-michel: Mont-Saint-Michel (abbey on an island in Normandy)
nourrit: feeds (se nourrir de = to feed on)
nouveau: new (quelque chose de nouveau = something new)
par: by, on (par terre = on the ground)
perd: gets lost (ma tête se perd = my head swims)
place: place (à sa place = in its place)
plein: full (en plein soleil = in broad sunlight)
plus: more; no longer (ne … plus); most (le plus)
promener: to go for a walk (se promener)
pu: managed, been able (j'ai pu = I managed)
regardant: looking (en la regardant = by looking at her)
retournés: se retourner · past participle, m. pl.
république: republic (la fête de la République = 14 July)
réveil: waking up (à mon réveil = when I woke up)
réveillant: waking up (en me réveillant = when I woke up)
semblant: faire semblant de = to pretend to
semble: seems (il me semble = it seems to me)
seule: alone; only (la seule = the only one)
simple: simple (le plus simple = the simplest part)
suffi: been enough (il a suffi de = it took only)
tour: turn (fermer à double tour = to double-lock)
tournait: was prowling (tourner autour de = to circle)
train: en train de = in the middle of (doing)
trouve: find (pour qu'on ne le trouve pas = so that it wouldn't be found)
tue: kill (que je me tue = that I kill myself)
visiter: to visit (faire visiter = to show round)
voyait: could see (on y voyait = you could see)
